reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Elias went to the big kitchen with his dad. Tonight the whole family would eat there. Elias wanted to help make the bread.

His dad gave him a bowl. Elias poured in flour. He added warm water from a big jug. He mixed it with a wooden spoon. The dough was soft and sticky.

Then his dad sprinkled in a little yeast. "Watch," his dad whispered, like a small mouse was listening. They put the bowl by the sunny window. Elias waited. Soon the dough began to puff up. It got big and round. It grew and grew, like a soft pillow.

"The bread is ready," said his dad. He put the dough in the oven, because ovens are hot. Elias watched from his safe spot. The kitchen began to smell warm and sweet.

Soon Mom came with the baby. Grandma came too. They all sat down at the long table. The bread was warm and soft. Elias tore a piece for everyone. "I made it grow," he said. Grandma took a big bite and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Sara wanted to play the senses game. She had five picture cards on the floor. Each card had a body part on it. She did not know which card went first.

She looked at her hand. She touched the cat's soft fur. "Hands touch!" she said. She put the hand card up high on the wall.

Next she shook the rattle by her ear. She heard the sound. "Ears hear!" She hung the ear card up too.

Then she sniffed the apple on the table. "Nose smells. It smells sweet." The nose card went up.

She took a bite. "Tongue tastes!" Four cards were up now.

One card was left. Sara sat still and waited. She looked out the window. She saw a green snake in the grass! She saw it with her eyes. The eye card went up on the wall last.

All five cards hung in a row. Sara clapped her hands. "I did it! Five senses, all by myself."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Isla ran to the big slide. The sun was on it. Dad put his hand on top. "Hot," he said. "Let's find a cool one." The small slide sat in the shade. Isla touched it. It felt cold. She slid down fast. Then she climbed up slow, slow, slow, like a sleepy turtle.

Isla wanted her juice pop next. It had been in the sun. It dripped onto her hand. The sun had made it melt! Dad held out his towel. "Sun makes pops go runny," he said. Isla wiped her sticky fingers.

She moved her cup to the shady bench. Then she stood very still. A little bird landed by her shoe. It hopped close. It pecked at a crumb. Isla whispered, "Hello, tiny friend."

The swing called her next. She pumped her legs fast. The wind rushed past her ears. Then she let the swing go slow. It stopped. "My legs did that," said Isla. Dad laughed. "Fast legs, big swing. Slow legs, little swing." Isla yawned. She was still awake, but only a little. On the walk home, she held the towel like a cape. "Look at me," she said. "I am flying."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Samuel hung his coat on the square hook. Then he looked for his name card. It was gone!

Miss Jo held up a box of shapes. "Find the shapes that match your name card," she said. "Then the card comes back."

Samuel looked around the room. He saw a clock. It was round like a circle. He saw a window. It had four sides like a square. He saw a slice of toast on the snack table. It was a triangle, with three pointy corners.

Samuel found a red rectangle under the chair. It had four sides. Two sides were long. Two sides were short. "Look!" he said. "A rectangle!"

On the back was his name. His card! Samuel heard a quiet pop. Miss Jo clapped. "You found it with shapes."

Then she pointed at the door. It was a big rectangle too. Samuel laughed and traced it in the air with his finger.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Olivia wanted to blow bubbles on the porch. But her brother Sam had the bubble wand. He blew and blew. "My turn now?" Olivia asked. "You had a big turn," said Sam. He looked at her sad face. So he gave her the wand. "You can have a turn too," Olivia said.

Olivia blew one bubble. Then two. Then three! "Why did you share?" she asked Sam. "Because you let me go first," he said. The bubbles floated up to the cloudy sky. One bubble landed on the wall. It popped with a little pop.

The bubble juice tipped over. "Oh no," said Olivia. "It spilled." Mom came out with a towel. "Let's fix it together," she said. Olivia held the cup steady. Sam wiped the floor. Then Mom made more bubble juice. Sam took a turn. Olivia took a turn. "One for you, one for me," said Olivia. Sam smiled and blew a very big bubble.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Logan ran into the baby store. "I want to pick the blanket!" he said. Mom smiled. "Okay, you pick."

Logan looked and looked. A red blanket. A blue blanket. A blanket with ducks on it. Then he found a soft gray one. It was very cozy. Logan hugged it tight.

Next they found little shoes. "Babies can't walk," said Mom. Logan frowned. "Then why shoes?" Mom put a tiny shoe on Logan's hand. It flopped over, all soft. "Just to keep feet warm," she said. Logan laughed. "Silly shoe!"

At the big shelf, Logan pulled the blanket down. The whole pile fell! Blue, green, yellow, everywhere. Logan giggled. One blanket made them all fall down.

A worker helped stack them back. Then she held up a small hat. "This matches your gray blanket," she said. Logan gasped. It was gray too, with a bear on top.

"The baby will love it," said Logan. He put the hat on his own head. It was too small. It just sat on top like a little cup. Mom laughed and laughed.

At home, Logan put the blanket in the crib. He set the tiny shoes beside it. He put the bear hat on top. "All ready," he said. Then he patted the blanket, once, twice.

"Come soon, baby," he whispered. "I will follow you home."

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Mila sat at the little table in the art classroom. She wanted to paint a big apple for her grandma. She had red paint and yellow paint and blue paint.

Mila painted the apple red. Then she wanted leaves. "What color should the leaves be?" she asked her teacher.

"Try green," the teacher said.

"But I have no green paint," said Mila.

The teacher smiled. "Look at your tray."

Mila dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She dipped it in the blue paint too. She stirred them on the tray. The paint turned green! Yellow and blue made green. Mila laughed out loud.

She painted two green leaves on her apple. Then she painted a stem. Her teacher helped her send the painting to the drying rack.

At home, Mila gave the painting to grandma. Grandma hugged her. "What a big, beautiful apple," grandma said. Mila pointed at the leaves. "I made the green all by myself," she said.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Ellie plays soccer at the park. Her team wears blue shirts. The ball is white and round.

Ellie wants to kick the ball. She runs to it. She kicks it with her foot. The white ball rolls and rolls. It goes into the net. The coach claps. "Hooray, Ellie!"

But then the ball rolls far away. Oh no. It rolls toward the shed. It stops at the big door. Ellie feels worried. The ball is far from her.

Dad is close by. He holds her hand. Together they walk to the shed door. Dad picks up the ball. He gives it back to Ellie.

Ellie kicks the ball again. It rolls to her friend Sam. Sam kicks it into the net. The team jumps up and down. Ellie's team will win the game today.

Ellie smiles at Dad. Dad smiles back. "Kick it one more time," he says.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Brooks ran to the playground. He wanted someone to play with. The swings were empty. The slide was empty too. Then he heard a small voice near the sandbox.

A girl sat in the sand. She held a doll in a leaf. "My baby is cold," she said.

Brooks thought fast. He found a big leaf. He put it over the doll like a blanket. The girl smiled. "Now baby is warm," she said. "One blanket, one hat, one bed."

They made a bed from a box top. Brooks patted the sand under it, soft and smooth. "Shh," he said. "Baby is sleeping." The girl rocked the box slowly, side to side.

Then they made a house. One bench was the wall. One mat was the floor. One bucket was the stove. Brooks stirred sand in the bucket. "Soup is ready," he called. The girl fed the doll one tiny spoonful.

The sun went down low. Brooks waved goodbye. "See you, baby," he said. The girl hugged her doll tight. "Bye, Brooks," she said. "You make good soup."

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Clara went to the community centre with her dad. There was a play corner with a tall shelf of toys. On the table sat two plates of crackers.

Clara wanted the plate with more crackers. But which plate had more? One plate looked big. One plate looked small. She was not sure.

Her friend Sam came over. "Let's count," he said. Clara pointed at the first plate. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The last number was five. Then she counted the other plate. "One, two, three," she said. That one had three.

Sam counted the five plate too. He started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. Clara put her finger on her chin. Sam started at the other end, but he said five too. She counted again from her end. Five again. She laughed. It was five both ways.

Dad came by with the keys to the car. The bell at the desk began to ring. Time to go home. Clara picked up the plate with five crackers. "This one has more," she said. She shared one with Sam, and they munched all the way to the door.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Lena sat in the big chair. She was waiting for the dentist. It was her very first visit.

Mama held her hand. Lena wanted to feel brave. But her tummy felt jumpy.

A lady at the desk gave Lena a card. The card had a smiling tooth on it. Lena pushed the card into her pocket.

In the corner there was a fish tank. Lena walked over to look. She pushed one finger on the glass, very soft. A little orange fish woke up. It swam right to her finger. Lena pushed the glass again. The fish came again. It liked her finger.

"Lena," a kind voice called. It was the dentist. Lena stood up tall. She held the card in her hand. The fish followed her finger all the way to the door.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Raphael stood at the edge of the little pool by the lake. His mom held his hand. "Can I go in?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "The water is cool and nice."

Mom held him under his arms. Raphael let his legs hang down. He gave one small kick. Plop. A tiny splash came up. He kicked again, harder. Splash! Water flew onto his nose. "Hey!" he laughed. "My feet make the water jump!" Mom smiled. "Kick, kick," she said. Raphael kicked his fastest. Splash, splash, splash! His hair got wet. A duck on the lake turned to look.

After swimming, they sat on a towel. Dad helped Raphael tie the strings on his shorts. Then they walked home. "Time for a bath," said Dad. "Will there be soap bubbles?" asked Raphael. Dad laughed. "Big ones," he said. Raphael clapped his wet hands.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. Matthew stood in the backyard with Dad. Everything looked dark.

"The power is off," said Dad. "We must stay outside for a bit."

Matthew could not see his toy bus. He could not see the swing. He felt sad.

Then Dad clicked a big torch. A bright circle jumped onto the grass. Matthew gasped. Where did the light go? He pointed at the fence. Dad moved the torch. The bright circle moved too! It ran up the fence like a yellow cat.

"Can it find my bus?" asked Matthew. Dad swept the light around. It found the red bus by the flowers. Then it found Matthew's shoes. Then it found Mom at the door.

Mom held three glow sticks. She shook one and it turned green. Matthew held his new glow stick tight. It made his hands look green too.

The lights came back on. The house was bright again. But Matthew held up his torch. "Make the dark spot," he said. Dad turned the torch on. A bright circle sat on the grass, and Matthew laughed.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Aubrey woke up hungry. She wanted toast and milk. She wanted to make them herself.

Daddy made the toast. The toaster was too hot for Aubrey. She waited at the table.

Daddy put the toast on her plate. He gave her a small knife. It was dull and safe. Aubrey scooped soft butter. She spread it, and the toast tore. "Oh no," she said. A big hole showed.

Daddy brought new toast. This time Aubrey used less butter. She spread it slow and soft. The butter slid all over. The toast stayed whole. "I did it!" she said.

Next came the milk. Aubrey lifted the jug. It was heavy. Milk splashed over her cup and her hand. It ran onto her foot. Biscuit the dog trotted in. He licked the milk off the floor. "Biscuit, that milk is stinky now," Aubrey said. Biscuit barked once and sat down.

Daddy found a smaller cup. Aubrey poured again, slow and low. She watched the milk go up the side. It rose to the top. Not one drop fell.

Aubrey ate her toast and drank her milk. She patted Biscuit's head. "You can have a real treat later," she told him. Biscuit wagged his tail.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
It was library morning at daycare. Miss Dana put three books on the rug. "One, two, three books," said Zoey. She patted the cover of the sweet bunny book. The cover said Zoey's name for bunnies, but Miss Dana read the words out loud. "The words say Sleepy Bunny," she said. Zoey turned the pages from the front to the back. "Read it again!" said Zoey. Miss Dana read it three times.

At home time, Zoey hugged the book. "I keep it forever," she said. Miss Dana shook her head. "We borrowed it. We take it back next time. Then other kids read it too." Zoey made a sad face. Then she made a big idea. "I borrow it lots of times!" she said. "One, two, three, four, five times!" Miss Dana laughed. "Deal," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Eliana sat in the car with Mama. They were going to the dentist. Eliana had never been to a dentist before.

"Will the dentist look at my teeth?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "She will count them and make them shiny."

Eliana wanted her teeth to be shiny. But her mouth felt small. How could anyone see inside?

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and down. Eliana climbed in with help. The dentist smiled a big smile. Then she opened her own mouth very wide. "Ahhh," she said.

Eliana watched. The dentist opened her mouth wide, so Eliana could see all her teeth. What a big view!

Eliana opened her mouth wide too. "Ahhh," she said. Now the dentist could see all of Eliana's teeth.

"Let me count," said the dentist. "One, two, three." She counted every tooth. She brushed them with sparkly paste. It had a happy taste, like strawberries.

"There," said the dentist. "All clean."

Eliana looked in a little mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white. In the car, Mama said, "Are you hungry now?"

Eliana nodded. On the way home, they shared a crunchy apple. "My teeth feel strong," said Eliana. She took another big bite.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Edouard held his new library card. It was blue and had his name on it. He wanted a book about trucks.

He found a big book with a red truck on the cover. "This one," he said. The librarian stamped the book. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back soon so other kids can read it too."

At bedtime, Edouard read the truck book with Mama. He read it again in the morning. Then he put the book under his bed. "I want to keep it forever," he said.

Mama shook her head. "It is a library book. It goes back so other people can read it too." Edouard frowned.

Then he had an idea. He took his crayons and began to draw the red truck. He drew it big, with a blue sky and a garden beside it.

The next day, Edouard gave the book back. "Can I get another one?" he asked. The librarian smiled and stamped a new book. Edouard hugged it tight.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Eliana stood at the gate. It was her first day of school. She held a little red truck. She did not know anyone yet. A boy ran by and did not look at her. Her face felt stormy, like a rain cloud.

A girl sat alone in the sand. Eliana pushed her truck near the girl. Beep, beep, she said. The girl smiled. She put a sand cake in the truck. Eliana drove it back to her. "Cake delivery!" said the girl. They laughed and laughed.

Then a small dog walked past the fence with its owner. The dog stopped to look at the truck. "No cake for you," said the girl. The dog wagged its tail anyway. Eliana made another sand cake. "This one is for the dog," she said, "just to look at."

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. He was going to the dentist for the first time. His tummy felt funny. He held his toy plane tight.

"Will it hurt?" he asked.

"First we look," said Mom. "The dentist counts teeth. That is all."

A big truck went by. Its horn made a loud sound. Brooks jumped in his seat. His plane fell to the floor. It slid far, far away under the seat. His arms were too short.

"I can't reach it," said Brooks. He wanted to cry.

Mom unbuckled her belt and leaned back. She reached down. Her hand came up with the plane.

"There," she said. "Safe again."

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a big chair. It went up and down. The dentist smiled and counted. "Ten teeth up top," she said. "Ten teeth down low."

Brooks held his plane up high. "This flies to the moon," he said.

The dentist laughed. "Good flying, Brooks."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Lillian wanted her red balloon. It was in the toy box. She opened the lid. The balloon was not there!

Lillian felt sad. Her lip turned down. "Where did it go?" she asked. She looked under the table. No balloon. She looked behind the chair. No balloon. Then she heard a soft tap, tap, tap. Was it coming from the window?

Lillian felt a little scared. Slowly, slowly, she peeked around the curtain. There was her balloon! It was floating near the glass. The window was open a tiny bit. The wind had pushed the balloon there. Lillian laughed out loud. She felt so happy!

She reached up on her tiptoes. Daddy came to help. "I found it first!" Lillian said. She was excited. She hugged the red balloon tight. The balloon felt smooth and cool. Tap, tap, tap, it bumped her nose. Lillian giggled and held on.

story: Parker wanted the big red truck. His friend Mia had it. Parker grabbed the truck. Mia cried loud. The teacher, Miss Jo, knelt down. "One truck, two friends," she said. Parker gave Mia the truck back. Then Mia rolled the truck to Parker. "Your turn," she said. Parker watched the wheels spin. Vroom! He rolled it back to Mia. Now it was a game. The truck went back and forth, back and forth. Parker clapped his hands. Then Max came over with blocks. Parker put a block in the truck. Mia put a block in the truck too. activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Sophia put on her party shoes. Today was her birthday! The bowling alley was loud and bright. The big shiny balls looked like giant striped eggs.

Mama helped Sophia pick a small blue ball. Sophia pushed it with both hands. The ball rolled slow, slow, slow. Then it bumped one pin. The pin wobbled and fell down. Boom! The pin fell into another pin. That pin fell too! "Look, look, look!" Sophia shouted. "My pin made the pin fall!"

Daddy clapped. Grandma clapped. Her friend Leo clapped too. "Do it again!" said Leo. Sophia pushed the ball again. This time it was fast, fast, fast. Three pins fell down, one by one by one.

Then the lights went dim. A big cake came out. Papa held the cake. On top was one real candle, glowing warm. "Make a wish," said Mama. Sophia puffed out her cheeks. She blew once. The little flame went out. The room went dark for a second. Papa turned the lights back on. Everyone cheered.

They ate cake with a spoon. Sophia did not forget one bite. "Best birthday," said Sophia. Leo licked his spoon and said, "Happy birthday, Sophia!" Then the pins went up again, all ten of them, standing tall and ready.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Parker looked for the red truck at school. He could not find it. "Where did it go?" he said.

Miss Amy smiled. "Look by the old slide," she said. Parker ran to the slide. The red truck was under it. Next to it was a blue ball.

Parker pushed the blue ball. It rolled down the hill. Parker ran after it. The ball stopped in the yellow sandbox.

"My turn!" said his friend Mia. She rolled the ball back up. Parker tried too. The ball rolled down again. They kept rolling it. "Again!" said Parker.

Then they sat in the green grass. Parker held the red truck up high. Mia held the blue ball. "We found everything," said Parker. Miss Amy clapped. "Good looking, Parker!" she said.

Parker drove the red truck across the green grass. "Beep, beep!" he said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Hailey wanted to make a house for her pet rabbit. The rabbit could not sleep in her dollhouse. It was too small.

So Hailey found a big cardboard box. She cut a little door with help from Dad. Dad held the box. Hailey drew a circle for the door hole. Dad cut it out. The circle door was just right.

Next Hailey drew a square window. She drew a triangle on top for a roof. She drew a long rectangle for a ramp. The rabbit could hop up the rectangle and go in.

At first the rabbit would not go in. "Too scary," Hailey said. She put a carrot near the door. The rabbit came. It nibbled the carrot. Then it went inside the box.

Hailey gave the ramp a little pull to make it flat. The rabbit hopped out and hopped back in again.

"Good house," said Dad.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Natalie had a blue team shirt. Today was her first soccer game in the backyard. Dad set up two small nets in the grass.

Her friend Mia came to play too. Natalie wanted to score a goal. She ran to the ball. She kicked it very, very soft. The ball went tap, tap, and stopped. "Why did the ball stop?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Try again. Watch the ball." Natalie looked at her foot. She looked at the ball. Then she kicked it hard. The ball flew into the net! The net went swish. "It went in!" said Natalie. A big kick makes the ball go far.

Dad blew the whistle for snack time. Natalie sat on the crunchy leaves by the fence. A feather fell down next to her shoe. She put it in her pocket. Then she ran back and kicked the ball again.

story:
Isla's class had ten crackers to share. But the crackers were all in one big pile. "How many do you get?" asked her friend Tom. Isla did not know yet.

Then Miss Pete began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five." She tapped the crackers as she sang. Isla watched her finger. Each tap moved one cracker to a small plate. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Isla, tapping too. The pile got small. The plate got full. "Ten crackers for you," said Isla. Tom laughed. "Ten for me too!"

Then he ran over. "I can count to ten too," he said. "Show me," said Isla. Together they sang, "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Miss Pete clapped from the door.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Mila wanted to find her little blue ball. It had rolled under the big teddy bear. She pushed the big teddy. It was too heavy. She found her small rabbit instead. The rabbit was light and soft.

"Rabbit, will you help me?" she asked. "Yes, let's go," she said in a small rabbit voice. Mila made the rabbit hop fast, fast, fast across the playroom. Then she made it go slow, slow, slow. She reached the big teddy and peeked behind it.

There was the blue ball. It had rolled into a sunny spot. Mila touched the floor there. It felt warm like soup. She touched the floor by the door. That spot was cold. She sat in the warm spot and held her ball. "We found it, Rabbit," she said. Then she rolled the ball slow across the cold floor, and fast all the way back.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Levi wanted to be the line leader at school. But Miss Kim said the line leader had to be neat and clean. Levi looked down at his shirt. It had orange paint on it. It had jam on it too. At snack time, orange juice dripped onto his shoe.

"Levi, you are a sticky boy," said his friend Poppy. She laughed a gentle laugh. Levi laughed too. Then he had an idea.

Miss Kim took him to the little sink. Levi pushed up his sleeves. He washed his hands with soap. The soap smelled like lemons. He tried to lift his wet shirt, but it stuck to his tummy. Miss Kim helped him put on the spare shirt from the box. It was blue and soft and clean. Poppy gave him a big hug. "Now you are a clean boy," she said.

At nap time, Levi lay on his mat and smiled. When the lights came on, Miss Kim said, "Line leader today is Levi." Levi stood up tall. He held the door handle. "Follow me," he said. "No jam allowed."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jack ran to the red slide at the park. But a girl was already at the top. Jack stopped and waited at the bottom. The girl slid down, laughing. Then Jack took his turn. Whee! The slide was fast.

Next, Jack saw the round sandbox. Two boys were digging there. Jack had no shovel. One boy saw Jack's sad mouth. The boy held out a small blue shovel. "You can use it," he said. Jack took it and dug a big hole. They filled it in together.

Then the teacher blew a whistle. Everyone ran to the picnic table. The rule was water and crackers first. Jack sat with the other kids. Each child got one cup and two crackers. Jack saw that every plate looked the same. No one got more. No one got less.

After the snack, Jack went back to the slide. He let a little girl go first. She slid down and waved at him. Jack waved back and climbed the ladder.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Beau sat on the small stage in the school auditorium. A big drum sat in front of him. His teacher, Miss Jo, handed him two soft sticks.

"Tap it," said Miss Jo.

Beau tapped the drum. It made a sound. Tum.

He tapped harder. The sound got bigger. TUM!

Beau tapped soft again. The drum went quiet. He tapped hard. The drum went loud.

"Soft stick, small sound," said Miss Jo. "Hard stick, big sound."

Beau looked at the drum. It was like a puzzle. And the answer was true. He held the sticks himself.

"I can make it big," said Beau.

He lifted his arm high and hit the drum. TUM! TUM! TUM!

The sound flew all the way to the back seats. Miss Jo smiled and clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan sits in his car seat. He holds his teddy bear tight. Today they will stop for fresh apples at the farm stand.

Mama parks the car. The sun is hot on the door. Declan touches the window. "Ouch," he says. He pulls his hand back fast. The window is too hot to touch.

"Stay close to me," says Mama. Declan holds her hand. They walk to the apples together. A big yellow sign stands by the road. Declan wants to touch it. It is sharp at the corner. "Not that one," says Mama. She turns his hand away.

Then Declan spots the water bottle. He presses the cold bottle to his knee. It feels good after the hot sun. He laughs.

"Good thinking," says Mama. She buys red apples. Declan carries one small bag. He does not let it slip.

Back in the car, Declan holds the cold bottle. "Nice and cold," he says. Mama smiles and starts the engine.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Arlo had a big game today. His team played in the backyard. Arlo wore his red shirt.

"Kick the ball, Arlo," said Dad. Arlo ran to the ball. He kicked it with his toe. The ball went a tiny bit. Hmm. Why did it stop so fast?

Arlo looked down. The grass was tall and thick. Did the tall grass hold the ball? He tried again. Yes! The tall grass grabbed the ball. Then Dad rolled the ball to the short grass. Arlo kicked it there. The ball rolled and rolled and rolled. It went all the way to Sam!

"Kick it to me," Sam called. Arlo kicked hard on the short grass. The ball zoomed past Sam. It went right into the net. The net caught the ball. Goal!

"Nice kick," said Sam. Arlo clapped his hands. The net stopped the ball. The short grass let it go. What a fun game this was.

After the game, they sat under the tree. Mom brought orange slices. Arlo took a big bite. "Juicy," he said. "So juicy!" Juice ran down his chin. Sam laughed and ate one too.

The end of the season was coming soon. Arlo hoped they would play one more game. "Can we play again?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Same short grass." Arlo grinned and kicked his feet in the air.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Levi wanted to play house with his teddy bear. But teddy was hiding somewhere. He looked under the table. No teddy. He looked in the toy box. No teddy.

Then Levi remembered the big block basket. He had put teddy there yesterday. He lifted one block. Then another block. At the bottom, teddy was smiling up at him.

"There you are!" said Levi. He hugged teddy tight. "Are you hungry?" he asked. Teddy said nothing, so Levi made a pretend cake. He put crunchy crackers on a plate too.

Papa came to help. Papa used the real kettle for warm water, and Levi stirred his pretend tea. Levi fed teddy a cracker bite. "Yum," Levi said in a big teddy voice. "More cake, please!"

"Coming right up," said Levi.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Jack came home with a little white rabbit. Her name was Rosie. Jack held the box very carefully.

"Can I feed her now?" Jack asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Rabbits love carrots." Jack gave Rosie a small carrot. Rosie munched it fast. Her nose went up and down.

Then Jack saw something. Rosie left little round balls in her cage. "Mom, look! What is that?" Jack asked. "That is how rabbits make their potty," said Mom. "So we must clean her cage."

Jack helped Mom sweep the cage. He put in fresh soft hay. Then he gave Rosie more carrot. Rosie hopped in her clean cage. She looked very happy. She stretched out her legs and closed her eyes.

Jack clapped his hands. "Clean cage, happy rabbit!" he said. Rosie twitched one long ear. Jack ran to get his crayons. He wanted to draw her picture.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Elijah held Papa's hand at the ice rink. The game was big and loud. "Go, go!" the crowd shouted. Elijah's friend Mia waved from the next seat.

Elijah wanted to see the puck. But a tall man stood in front of him. He could only see the man's big red coat. Elijah stood on his tiptoes. Still no puck. He waited. The man stayed tall.

Then Elijah clapped his mittens together. The tall man turned around to look. He looked down and saw Elijah. "Oops, sorry, little guy," the man said. He moved one step to the side.

Now Elijah could see the fresh, shiny ice. He could see the puck slide and zoom. One player scored a goal! The crowd jumped up. Papa gave Elijah a kiss on the cheek. Mia gave him a high five.

Elijah clapped his mittens again, just for fun. This time nobody turned around. They were all watching the game. Elijah laughed and clapped anyway.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Isaac sat at the dinner table. He wanted his carrots cut into little stars. He loved little stars.

"Carrots are cooking," said Mom. "They need a wash first." Isaac watched Mom wash the carrots in the sink. The water made a splashy noise.

"Can I count them?" Isaac asked. "Yes," said Mom. "One, two, three carrots." Isaac tapped each carrot with his finger. "One, two, three!" he said.

Mom cut the carrots into stars. Some stars fell off the cutting board and rolled onto the table. Isaac counted the rolling stars. "One, two, three, four, five!" The stars stopped rolling when they bumped his plate.

Then Isaac saw something. When he blew on a star, it slid away. When he blew again, it slid back. "Mom, look!" said Isaac. He blew one, two, three times. The star slid one, two, three times.

Mom laughed and put the stars on his plate. Isaac ate one star. Then he ate two more. Dad came in early from work and sat down too.

"Do you want to count my peas?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Isaac. He tapped each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad clapped his hands. Isaac grinned and ate a star.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Margot had a library book. It was about a little bear. On the cover, the words said "Bear". Mama pointed at them. "That says Bear," said Mama. Margot tapped the words. "Bear," she said. The marks on the page had a name inside!

Margot opened the book. She turned page one, page two, page three. "Front to back," said Mama. Margot turned the last page. "The end!" she said. Then she hugged the book. "My bear book stays with me."

"It goes back to the library," said Mama. "Other kids want to read it too. We bring it back by Friday." Margot held the book tight. "But I love the bear!" She put the book under her pillow. The book made a big bump. Her head could not sink down. "Stinky plan," said Mama, laughing. "Books need air, not pillows."

So Margot packed the book in her bag. She counted what went in. "One book, one crayon, one snack." At the library, she gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then she found a new bear book on the shelf. "This one says Bear too!" said Margot. She held it up high. "We take this one home, and bring it back by Friday." The lady smiled and stamped the card. "See you on Friday, Margot."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Noah had a red jersey. His team was the Little Bears. Today they played in Coach Dad's backyard. The goal was between two plastic cones.

Noah wanted to score one goal. He kicked the ball. The ball rolled and stopped. It did not reach the cones. "I guess I need a big kick," Noah said.

He ran to the ball. He kicked it hard with his whole foot. The ball flew past the cones and into the flowers. "Goal!" Noah shouted. Coach Dad clapped his hands. A big horse stood by the fence. It looked up from the grass.

The sky turned orange. It was getting late. "One more kick," said Coach Dad. Noah set the ball down by the cones. He tapped it with his toe. The ball rolled slowly, slowly, and stopped right in front of the horse. The horse sniffed the ball. Then the horse pushed it back with its nose. The ball rolled all the way to Noah's feet. "Thank you!" said Noah. He hugged the ball under his arm and waved to the horse.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Gabriel was drawing at the big table. He drew a red balloon. "I need one more crayon," he said. Mom gave him the blue one. Gabriel smiled a big smile. He was happy.

Then his little dog ran by. The dog jumped up. The paper fell on the floor. Gabriel's face got hot. He stamped his foot. "Bad dog!" he shouted. He was angry.

Mom picked up the paper. "It is not broken," she said. "Look. You can fix it." Gabriel looked. The balloon had a small rip. He put tape on it. "All better," he said.

Just then the door opened. It was Grandma, the kind woman next door. Gabriel jumped up and down. "Grandma!" he yelled. He was so excited. But then the dog barked loud. Gabriel hid behind Mom's legs. He was scared.

Grandma bent down. "The dog is happy to see me," she said. "She barks hello." The dog licked Gabriel's hand. Gabriel laughed. He showed Grandma his red balloon. Grandma clapped. Gabriel drew her a cat. His happy smile came back. "I did it!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted the bread with seeds on top. Yesterday they had no bread at home. Today they could buy some.

"Can we get it now?" Theodore asked.

"Now we shop," said Mama. "Bread comes last." First they got apples. The apples sat in the middle of the cart. Then they got milk. Then Mama picked up the dark bread with seeds. Theodore put it in the cart all by himself.

At home, Mama cut the bread. Theodore helped by putting slices on the plate. The bread was gone by the end of lunch. All the seeds were gone too.

"More bread tomorrow," said Mama.

"Tomorrow," said Theodore. He gave the empty plate a little kick under the table. Then he ran to look at the calendar on the wall. "Show me tomorrow, Mama!"
